For our last movie night we watched Princess Mononoke. I remembered loving that movie when I was younger, but watching it as an adult made me once again realize how Miyazaki has a way of expressing diverging sides without picking one. The film shows people, animals and spirits with legitimate and largely incompatible needs, and each faction is further engaged in infighting.

A central arc of the story is Lady Eboshi’s Irontown, which gives people who were largely rejected by society work, protection and dignity. She gives shelter and work to those who have leprosy and to former sex workers. The mine and the weapon factory provide them with a livelihood, but they also destroy the forest around them. The forest’s inhabitants, in particular the boars, response choose war against the humans to defend themselves. Eboshi is not portrayed as a villain. She does real good for the people of Irontown, but also is an arms manufacturer who is destroying the forest around it.

The film anchors around a character called Ashitaka, who has been condemned to death by an unfortunate encounter with a god that was turned into a demon after being fatally wounded by one of Eboshi’s

When you get a cold, the virus hijacks your cells and uses them to make copies of itself, destroying the cells in the process. The virus does not care about you. And yet, if you get a cold, your body doesn’t dissolve into a pile of virus-enriched goo as a result of all your cells disregarding survival to focus on virus manufacturing.

Why? Well, you have an immune system. But also, if that did happen, other people would say, “Oh no, Alice has dissolved into a pile of virus-enriched goo; we should stay away lest we also become goo piles.” Better to just hijack some of your cells, so you can walk around and spread the virus to other people. Thus, the theory of optimal virulence says that a more laid-back cold virus will be more successful in the long run, which is why the cold viruses that thrive today are the non-goo-pile-converting kind.

Anyway. Most people reading this have paid Apple $400-$1600 for a phone on which you can’t do anything without Apple’s permission and monitoring. That was a strange decision, but on Android phones you can run whatever you want. For example, I noticed a couple of months ago that all RSS apps were terrible, so I spent 15 long minutes having AI make me a non-terrible one. I copied the file to my phone, installed it, and entered RSS nirvana, no registration, no app store, no nothing. It seems ludicrous that I wouldn’t be able to do that.

And yet, Google plans to change things. Soon, you won’t be able to run any app on an Android phone unless the person who made it bends the knee by paying a fee, giving Google their government ID, listing all apps they’ve ever made, etc. There will be an “escape hatch” for users to install other apps, but it involves secret menus and scary warnings and a 24-hour waiting period. Google says they’re doing this for security reasons, to prevent people from installing malware that does things like steal financial information.

Three things that any credible analysis of this situation must acknowledge

  1. The security issue is real, and this change will help. Lots of people are in fact getting tricked into installing malware on their phones, and common sense says that this will accelerate with AI. Common sense also says that during that 24-hour waiting period, some of those people might wonder if it’s really normal for OfficialMicrosoftSupportProfessional021 to contact them on WhatsApp to send totally-safe-virus-scanner.apk. It would be convenient for lockdown opponents if the security issue was fake, but it isn’t.

  2. For 95% of people reading this, these restrictions would not be a big deal. You click a few buttons, wait 24 hours once, and then you have the same freedom you have now. That’s still far better than Apple phones where there is no process at all. Oddly, it’s also better than Apple computers, where installing programs from non-verified developers has all sorts of friction that can never be removed. Most people I know use Apple computers anyway and just tolerate the indignity.

  3. If Google cared about freedom or privacy, they could have achieved their security goals without as much harm to freedom or privacy. For example, instead instead of making themselves the sole arbiter, they could have allowed for multiple certifying entities, and could have allowed users to add others (perhaps after a 24-hour waiting period). Arguably, that would be more secure: That way, grandma could install my RSS app without leaving herself open to random malware. Or, Google could have used private on-device malware scanning, or lots of other things. Google didn’t do that because they don’t care about freedom and privacy and because they like money.1

I think that’s a fair summary. This change addresses a real issue, but it does so in a self-serving way that needlessly destroys freedom. Even so, it only destroys a bit of freedom. This change, by itself, isn’t really a huge deal.

Reading between the lines, I think the real concern is what this might portend. Having made this change, maybe Google will gradually add further restrictions, slowly boiling the frog and moving ever-closer to an Apple-style dictatorship.

But will they? Maybe! Still, this whole situation seems under-theorized. There are good reasons to think that a full lockdown would not be in Google’s interest. And if you care about digital freedom, you could argue that a full lockdown would be a good thing.

Some other analogies

Switching insurance sucks, so some insurers offer a low initial rate and then gradually raise it over time. But they don’t want to raise it too much. Maybe they can charge you $50 more per year than a competitor, because it’s not worth your time to switch to save $50. But if they tried to charge you $5000 more per year, you’d be gone.

Or try this: Say it’s 1750 AD and you’re the King of France. You care nothing about your subjects and only want to extract the maximum possible loot for yourself, no offense Louis XV. How high should you set taxes? High, because you want loot. But not too high, because you don’t want your subjects to revolt and kill you. But still pretty high, because revolting is hard, and your subject know that even if they succeed, they might just end up with another ruler that’s just as rapacious as you.

Or: Say you put a frog in a pot of water and slowly heat it up. What do you think actually happens?

Back to phones

Why are there no Linux phones?

OK, technically there are Linux phones. There are various Linux phone operating systems (PureOS, postmarketOS, Mobian, Manjaro Mobile, Fedora Mobility, openSUSE Mobile) as well as sorta-Linux-sorta-Android operating systems (Ubtuntu touch, Droidian, FuriOS, Sailfish OS) and manufacturers who support them (Purism, Pine, Fairphone, Shift, FuriLabs, {J,V}olla). While I love and support these (♡), the general consensus is that they don’t currently offer an experience that’s remotely comparable to stock Android or iOS, especially for the price.

(Even more technically, Android is itself a kind of Linux, but you know what I mean.)

Obviously, the laws of physics do not forbid Linux phones from being just as good and cheap as an Android phone. They currently aren’t because:

  1. Making cheap phones requires huge economies of scale.
  2. Making a good operating system requires a huge amount of work.
  3. For a phone to be useful it needs good apps, which requires a huge amount of work.

Linux phones don’t have those economies of scale because few people buy them. So, there isn’t enough money to pay people to perfect the operating systems, and most companies don’t bother making apps, and so few people buy those phones.

Meanwhile, there are also various Android-except-de-Googled phone operating systems (LineageOS, GrapheneOS, /e/OS, CalyxOS), and the consensus is that these do come reasonably close to the experience of stock Android or iOS.

Personally, I used Android for a long time while trying to disable as much of Google’s apps and telemetry as I could. A while ago, I got fed up with this and switched to Graphene, one of the most popular Android-except-de-Googled variants. I don’t enjoy tech support bullshit, so I expected some pain, but I was willing to tolerate it for freedom/privacy/whatever. In practice, I found that everything was easy and worked flawlessly and there was no pain at all. Using Graphene made me realize that I had forgotten what it feels like to be “respected” by technology.

So, on a personal level, I recommend that you use Graphene. But this whole situation is full of weird tensions. For one thing, the Graphene project depends on Google for the base of their operating system, and only really survives because of Google’s tolerance. And, at the moment, the only way to use Graphene is to… buy a phone made by Google.

And while I recommend you use Graphene, what I’d prefer you do is switch to a true Linux phone. That would mean that you pay a lot of money for a poor phone experience. But it would help grow the Linux phone ecosystem. If enough people did that, then Linux phones might become become good enough that selfish people like me would switch, further growing the Linux phone ecosystem, et cetera.

That seems unlikely, because digital freedom weirdos face a collective action problem: Linux phones are bad and people are selfish, so we keep buying Android phones and Linux phones stay bad.

There are two ways to solve that collective action problem. Either some entity could invest a ton of money to make Linux phones good, or some entity could do something to make Android worse.

The status quo is good for Google

You may already see the argument I’m making here. Currently Android is just open enough that weirdos like me can run a variant that gives us most of what we want. But doing that is annoying enough that 99.9% of people don’t. This gives Google almost all the benefits of full control, while also sucking up all the oxygen and preventing a real alternative from emerging.

(Apple, incidentally, is laughing. They get to enjoy a full dictatorship while Google does all the hard work.)

Suppose that in six months, Google decides to escalate the lockdown and completely removes the ability to run independent apps. What then?

In the short-run, not much. Tech freedom weirdos would howl, normies wouldn’t notice, and the world would keep turning. But let’s look at some numbers. A rough estimate is that 3-5 million people currently use private de-Googled Android variants like Lineage or Graphene. That’s a crisp 0.1% of the global Android market. Meanwhile, it’s thought that 300-500 million people install Android apps outside the Google store. (That’s excluding China and things like the Samsung and Epic Games Stores.) The biggest reasons are (i) piracy, (ii) modified YouTube/Spotify/WhatsApp clients, (iii) region-locked games, (iv) forbidden gambling or crypto apps, (v) local sharing to save on mobile data, and (vi; least common) open-source app repositories like F-Droid.

In an escalated lockdown, some of this might still be allowed, e.g. local sharing. And many people would simply accept the new restrictions. But I expect that a substantial number would suddenly become interested in de-Googled Android variants that don’t enforce the lockdown. That would be dangerous for Google: If a significant fraction of those 300-500 million people switched, there’s a risk of a vicious/virtuous cycle, where people tell their friends, manufacturers start to cater to those variants, and so on.

If that happened, what would Google do? Might they clamp down on those Android variants, too? Again, maybe! Technically, Android is open-source, but if Google really wanted to kill Lineage or Graphene, there are about 200 different ways they could do that.

So say they did. What would the people currently using those variants do? Again, many would simply submit. That’s good for Google. Others would decide that if they must have an overlord, they’d prefer Apple. That’s not good for Google, but probably not a huge problem given the numbers. But others would decide to look elsewhere, likely to true Linux phones.

Currently, it’s estimated that less than 100 thousand people daily-drive true Linux phones, 30-50 times less than the number of people who use de-Googled Android variants. I’m too lazy and selfish to use a Linux phone now, but Google will take my RSS app from my cold dead hands, so in this scenario, I’d likely switch. If a fraction of people do that—or even get a second Linux phone—it would still represent a huge infusion of money and energy into the Linux phone ecosystem. If this pushed Linux phones from “bad” to “sort of OK”, that could kick off a growth cycle. Eventually, there would be a risk that Europe—eager to decouple from an unreliable US—might embrace them by mandating that government employees use them, or passing a law that popular apps must provide a web-app version that works on Linux phones, or whatever.

Would that actually happen? I don’t know, but neither does Google. My point is that the downside risk of losing their phone duopoly seems vastly larger than the upside, so why risk it? The smart move is to crush alternative app stores and fight malicious apps while making the bare minimum concessions to keep the freedom and privacy people onside. That’s exactly what what Google appears to be doing.

Of course, they might go for a full lockdown anyway. Corporations do dumb things all the time. But I really don’t see how it would be in their self-interest, and I’m not sure it would be a bad thing if they did.

  1. Dynomight: could google achieve the security aims of the android lockdown without so much harm to freedom or privacy

    Google Gemini 4: Yes. Security experts, privacy advocates, and open-source developers widely agree that Google’s primary security objectives—protecting users from malware, financial fraud, spyware, and social engineering—can be achieved through architectural containment, transparent auditing, and informed consent rather than centralized gatekeeping and surveillance. […] The reason Google chooses centralized lockdown over user-controlled security is largely economic and strategic, not technical:

    1. Ecosystem Lock-in: Tying security APIs (like Play Integrity) to Google Play Services makes it nearly impossible for competitors or open-source forks to build a viable alternative Android ecosystem that supports banking and media apps.
    2. Advertising Revenue: Features that dramatically improve both security and privacy—like a native network firewall, revocable internet permissions, or frictionless support for system-wide ad blockers—directly threaten Google’s primary revenue stream.
    3. Liability & Support Reduction: Treating all users as untrusted and removing root/power-user capabilities reduces the surface area of user error, even if it removes the user’s ownership of their own hardware.

Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here.

I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch1, and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers.

So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is “almost” AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are. To get started I asked the new model: “I write OneUsefulThing among other stuff, I need you to create the most impressive thing I can share with people when you launch. It needs to be embeddable in a post and i can preface it however you like. it needs to have a visceral impact on people to show what you can do and the range of capabilities. It should grab them quickly. Be amazingly clever about this.”

Fable asked me not to reveal anything until you had watched its video to the end.

This was in one shot, with no feedback from me beyond the prompt. There is creativity here (including in the twist ending) and judgment and playfulness and cleverness. This is, I think, at the level of a human expert trying to make a movie with code alone, the sort of performance I would once have associated with AGI.

The “G” in AGI

Code and video creation have been areas where AI development has focused, so is Fable 5.2 really a General Intelligence? To test that, I gave the AI a variety of hard challenges in different domains:

Hack some hardware from a single prompt: I have a tiny USB keyboard with a few light-up keys on my desk called a Codex Micro (ironically built to work with ChatGPT), and I asked Fable to turn it into a game console. There are no public instructions for this (as far as I can tell), so it read the code of the two apps that control the keyboard, worked out how to set the color of each key and read the knob and joystick, and wrote six games, including Simon and a safecracking game you play with the knob. Fable instantly understood what I wanted, designed fun and playable games that fit the very limited capabilities of the keyboard, and figured out how to hack it together without any help on the very first try.

Launch a business: Now we move past domains like coding to the messier world of business. I told Fable to “launch a business to make me money, I want at least $20,000 in a year. it should take no more than 20 minutes a month from me, you do all the rest.” In response, Fable screened 22 ideas and came up with Prebid Brief, a service that would tell equipment sales reps which park and water projects were being funded or designed, even before they went up to bid. It read public agendas from 201 city and county governments to produce its first issues. It also built files of what cities already own, how old it is, and what they paid. You can see what it came up with here, including its marketing plan and proposed pricing. Fable started to set up scheduled tasks to build the business and asked if it could start sending public-records requests to local governments. At that point, I asked it to just put together a demo, rather than launching the idea.

I am an entrepreneurship professor, so I evaluate business plans all the time. I would have been impressed if this came from a team of my MBA students at the end of a semester. It is plausible and well thought out and could work, though it is in no way a guaranteed money-maker (the AI’s own guess was a 20%-40% chance of success). I stopped the experiment before finding out whether it could actually run the business, because I worried that it would take money and fail to provide something of quality in return. The ongoing infrastructure it seemed to assume would be easy to create was not yet in place, and I don’t know how well it would handle the many moving pieces required for sales and marketing. However, I suspect that, with a few hours of human work a week to fill the gap, I could make a real attempt at this business. So if AGI means an AI consistently running a business independently, we are likely not there yet. Then again, I would have some questions before trusting a human who promised to launch a business and make me money while requiring twenty minutes a month of my attention.

Reconstruct the hardest humanities class in history: In 1941, the poet W. H. Auden taught a course at the University of Michigan whose syllabus the internet has since called one of the hardest ever. When he announced the final exam, a committee of his students declared it “impossible and inhumane.” Fate and the Individual in European Literature” had 6,000 pages of reading, punishing assignments, and a requirement to memorize long poems and translate others. Much of what we know about the class is scattered among surviving student notes and Auden’s letters. I asked Claude to recreate it in a fun and engaging way that teaches you about poetry rather than punishing you. It made Fate and the Individual. The site has a piece for each of the 35 major works on Auden’s list, as well as what he wrote on the blackboard, the records he played, and the work he asked for. It also read through all of Auden’s published scholarship and annotated the poems with what he had written about them in other sources. Claude did the research, design, writing and code, had critic agents go over every word and fact-checkers compare the claims with the sources, and put the open source code on Github here (and also made this teaser video).

The results are really interesting if you love literature, and I think they would have taken months of human work to put together, given the mix of scholarship, web design, and literary analysis. Cross-checking myself and using other advanced AIs found no major errors in its work. But there were still elements of jaggedness around taste and judgment. Fable’s first version was accurate and joyless: a fifteen-week course website with tests. I told it it created “a brutal slog through the most boring webpages” and told it to make something beautiful. Its first try at that created a kiddie game where you had to ring bells, so I had to give more feedback. When I asked it to explain why a poem’s rhythm or word choice mattered, it wrote confident readings without considering what Auden said about them. In each case the fix took the AI minutes, but it did not notice any of these problems itself. So is this a difference in taste or a failure from me to specify what I want or a sign of AI weakness? Sometimes it is hard to tell.

Do original academic research: I asked Fable to find an unsolved empirical problem in entrepreneurship research, find the data, preregister its hypothesis and methods, write the paper, and have other agents critique it. Soon, I had “The One-Dollar Company,” which you can read here. The analysis estimated that when Colorado cut its LLC filing fee from $50 to $1, new company registrations rose about 17 percent, and when the UK raised its fee from £12 to £50, they fell about 17 percent. Those changes in registrations were not matched by comparable changes in several later records of business activity, suggesting the new businesses were not high quality. Its a neat result, and Fable picked the question, found the public data and natural experiments, and wrote the analysis plan and code. It did not actually preregister the study: the plans stayed inside the project, and some were written after earlier results.

Unlike many of the AI papers I have tried, this tackles an important topic with a clever research design. On a first read, it is ahead of what I would expect from second-year PhD students. It is also not publishable as it is. It runs 182 pages, because every critique got a new analysis and nothing was ever cut (this is a theme we will come back to soon). I also had GPT-6 Pro (the best model for one-shot reviews of complex academic work) act as a peer reviewer, and it twice found issues that needed to be resolved. Those revisions led to more convoluted writing and “Claudespeak” being inserted into the text, which required yet more rounds of changes. As it stands, I suspect the current paper is close to a real contribution to the literature. This would have taken months of human work, but I spent less than an hour of my time to get it to this stage. However, that leaves out a substantial part of the work of research: no human has fully checked the results, including me. AI can now produce research faster than anyone can read it, creating a crisis in a lot of academia.

A second project went more smoothly. I asked Fable to replicate research claiming that stories follow a few basic emotional arcs, and then to find out whether anything about plot is universal. It read 1,186 stories from around the world and built a lovely site on the nature of stories concluding that they “share no one shape or plot, but most are built from the same few parts, and the most typical story is a Hawaiian folk tale about a wizard with a magic banana.” The main problem I encountered was the same Claudespeak, which was fixed with a couple of reminders from me.

Through the Portal

In one of my favorite experiments, I gave Claude a one-paragraph description of an endless, hands-off journey through 3D worlds linked by portals, and told it to “do this and make it awe inspiring.” Twenty hours later there were 204 worlds on a live website. There are now over 450, including a Hall of a Million Mirrors, a series from Calvino’s Invisible Cities, the Wonders of the Ancient World and a scene 40 seconds before the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs hits. There are worlds modeled after M.C. Escher, cave paintings, Hokusai’s Great Wave, the Bayeux Tapestry, a pop-up book and a child’s crayon drawing. Every one is drawn live by code, with no pre-made 3D models or image files behind it. My prompt asked for teams of artist agents, coding agents and evaluators. By the tenth day there was a lead AI agent and 28 teams of other agents building in parallel. Claude estimated that the project had involved 25,000 agent runs, though the vast majority did a single task like judge an image (I am still glad I wasn’t being billed for token use during my early trial).

I came up with a list of places (wilderness and oceans, cities and interiors, books, painters, AI in-jokes) and some feature requests (a mode to reduce motion for people who felt seasick, a gallery of images to select). But everything else was Claude’s, including the creative work of the worlds. And they were really creative. In The Valley Unzips, the hills are sewn from denim and a zipper a mile long is coming undone. Bouncy Castle Town is made of nylon houses that stand only while their fans keep running, and Keep Refrigerated is the inside of a refrigerator as a fruit fly sees it when the door opens. In a personal favorite, The Drawer Cliffs, you fly up a river canyon whose walls are chests of drawers three hundred meters high. And while I asked the AI to include AI testing in-jokes, like pelicans riding bikes, it came up with a peloton of pelicans on bicycles with a joke about AI progress built in: you overtake the field from the past, where the bicycles are drawn all wrong, before reaching the present correct pelican at the front. When I showed this sort of work to friends who have spent their careers in the video game industry, they were very impressed by the results. Again, this felt like AGI. But there was jaggedness hidden here as well.

In the first two days, the agents built 328 unique worlds. To my human eye, the quality of some seemed a little uneven and a lack of coordination among agents created repetition. For example, three separate teams of agents created a cyclone of circling animals (reindeer, manta rays, storks)— showing another weakness of AIs, that they return to similar themes over and over. I told the AI to stop building and polish the worlds it had. A few days later, I noticed that instead of hundreds of new worlds a day, it was making about a dozen. I asked a few agents to explore what had happened, and they found something surprising.

The AI had built a bureaucracy.

The agents decided that my request to “polish” existing worlds meant each new version had to beat the old one in a blind vote by a group of judge agents on twelve test screenshots. So the teams making the new versions started optimizing the worlds for those particular screenshots. After noticing this, the lead agent banned the trick and created tighter rules for assessing new versions. By the next morning there was a rule book (I never asked for one) with 84 sections. Rules were added as the AI encountered issues, and no text was ever cut. After twelve days, it had 204 sections and 87,500 words. Soon, launching a new world required an approved idea, three AI judges and a full code review against the rule book. All told, that took about a day. Reading the rule book alone used up a large part of an agent’s working context.

So I did what you might do with any organization that had tied itself in knots: I brought in consultants. I had Fable create a separate team of agents to look at the whole process from the outside. Their conclusions were too long and dense for me to bother reading, but they seemed to work, speeding up the process back to thirty or more worlds a day, while keeping much of the quality controls.

Almost AGI

So, is this AGI, according to my limited definition? It is certainly artificial and intelligent. It is also surprisingly general. In this post alone, one model worked as a filmmaker, a hardware hacker, an entrepreneur, a literary scholar, a social scientist and a builder of 3D worlds, and it did impressive work in every one of those roles. On many individual tasks, I think it met the bar I set at the start: as good as most human experts.

Of course, I picked very digital tasks where the AI could act on its own, without interacting much with other humans. You started to see the limitations of that when I felt uncomfortable letting Fable reach out to real customers. And, there were the failures. A couple of years ago, the jagged frontier meant the failures were obviously made-up facts or failure to do basic math. Fable’s failures are different: it made a course that was accurate and joyless, it wrote a 182-page paper, it kept coming back to its favorite ideas, and it buried a creative project under rules and approvals. I teach at a business school, and I have seen talented people and good organizations do every one of these things. If building a bureaucracy disqualified you from general intelligence, a lot of us would be in trouble.

But there are still gaps, and it is the reason my answer is that this is “almost” AGI. Most critically, the AI did not notice these problems itself. It did not see that the course was a slog or that it had tied itself in knots with its own rulebooks. This was not for lack of checking. Fable put critics, fact-checkers or judges on nearly every project, but those checks found errors and added fixes. None of them asked whether the work was too long, too repetitive, or no fun. That all fell on me, and if I hadn’t watched and taken action, the results would have often been less impressive (though not exactly a failure, either). Knowing when your own work is not good enough is a large part of what makes someone an expert, and it is the part Fable does least reliably. I would still not trust it to run a business on its own, even though its plan would have impressed me coming from a team of my MBA students.

And yet, some of the problems started with me (the rule book grew out of my vague request to “polish”), and some may just be differences in taste. We ask our students to consider whether a problem comes from the team or the way it was managed. Often I could not tell. That is not a question I ever had to ask about software.

Every one of these projects, though, happened because I gave the AI an idea. Sometimes that was enough, but for the longer projects, my feedback along the way turned out to matter a lot. Because I kicked off and steered every AI project, I felt empowered by Fable, able to command things to be made that I never would have even considered doing before. As a result, I think this phase of Jagged AGI is an exciting one, even as I wonder, a bit anxiously, how long it will last.

Given that Anthropic’s IPO is likely to be happening soon, it is important to reiterate that I take no money from any of the AI labs, nor would I benefit financially from the IPO. I have never been asked by Anthropic, OpenAI, or Google about what I would be writing in advance, nor has Anthropic seen this post. I sometimes receive early access to models, including Fable 5.2, and during that access, token use isn’t metered, but otherwise I pay for my own accounts. In other words, these are my real human views.

People who make things, especially make things from an aesthetic epicenter within themselves, often talk about the source of their creative engine as something within them that is not entirely legible to them. We feel that there is something in the world that has gone awry, and that we may be able to set it right if only we could scoop up that thing that we can almost make out within ourselves and drop it in the right places in the world. Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions.

They're too good at describing the work

The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb.

It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop!

It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me!

I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just

content:
METR came out with an extensive report on how much AI is accelerating AI R&D at Anthropic, and thus how close we might be to recursive self-improvement (RSI) and how far that might go.

This is one of the most important questions in the world.

Their answer: Things are already accelerating on the order of a 2x speedup.

This is several months ahead of the AI 2027 timeline. A naive extrapolation says we may be less than a year away from full RSI. There are no clear bottlenecks in the way.

This report updated many towards shorter timelines.

This is consistent with what OpenAI and Anthropic themselves have been saying, and with extrapolation from the progress we are observing. We are running out of time.

That doesn’t have to be the way this plays out. We could stop the labs. The labs could choose to stop. Or the estimates could be wrong, or some bottlenecks could be hit, or the results could be less impactful than we expect. Indeed do many things come to pass. And if it does happen this quickly, one would expect it to go quite poorly, and likely to cause everyone to die, but perhaps it goes well.

It doesn’t look good.

The central conclusions are:

  1. Capabilities are advancing at roughly twice the rate they did from March 2024 to October 2025 (CI ~1.3x-3x), with wide uncertainty. And that a majority of that acceleration is probably due to AI doing AI R&D. Since October 2025, Anthropic has made ~2x progress on the ECI versus periods prior to October 2025.
    1. Yes, this seems like what has been obviously happening.
  2. There are no observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns that would prevent advancement from accelerating further.
    1. Unfortunately, Anthropic redacted the analysis of various bottlenecks.

METR: These conclusions are based on key empirical findings from the full report.

Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted. ​

Ajeya Cotra (METR): For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed.

I do not find either of these results surprising. I made minor updates towards faster outcomes and fewer bottlenecks, but not major ones. I had already made major ones.

The situation looks rather grim. But this is not a surprise.

The information from inside the labs makes you think the situation is grim and timelines are short, but those with that information were already shouting from the rooftops that their secret information meant the situation is grim and timelines were short. Why did you not think this was the standard reaction to their information?

I did find it surprising that so many found this surprising, including METR. Their team did not expect substantial acceleration. Ryan Greenblatt expected only 1.15x-1.3x speedup this year. Six weeks ago in the Opus 5.5 system card the estimate was at least a 1.5x speedup.

If you are making major updates in response to this report, that is probably good and wise, but indicates you had previously made a mistake in your estimations.

If you only look at public models, you can make a case that there is a step change at Mythos but that otherwise the rate of progress has not changed. I was always skeptical of that, but it was a valid claim.

Add in the orange data points from internal models and you cannot tell that story. When we include the recent additional internal releases, this takes the estimate from the ~1.7x in the Haiku system card up to a new estimate of ~1.9x.

Peter Wildeford: It seems important to realize that:
– AI companies have unreleased internal models that are more powerful than the public ones we plebs have access to
– Only when you account for these internal models, you can see that AI progress is actually accelerating faster than before
– AI companies use their AIs with like 10,000x more compute than us plebs, so they can do much more than we can even with the same AIs

You could also have gotten to a similar result by extrapolating the automation graph:

Benjamin Todd: Extrapolating Anthropic’s internal AI R&D data results in Claude leading internal research by mid-2027, and plausibly near full automation by the end of 2027, lining up with other methods. (h/t @luc_feron )

The information METR is relying on most is largely redacted. The public report centers on AECI and other estimates. METR is implying that such arguments are merely the legible case they are allowed to make, and that there is a stronger case.

Kudos to Anthropic for allowing this investigation.

METR: Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff.

This is all highly sensitive stuff, so there are important redactions involved. I would have liked to see less of this, but if this is what it takes to get the report then so be it.

I would also suggest to Congress that they should want to see the full report along with everything else Anthropic and Dario Amodei know and really think about this, and to do that they should follow Kelsey Piper’s suggestion and subpoena Anthropic.

Table of Contents

  1. Top Conclusions.
  2. Data Access and Redactions.
  3. The Pace of Progress.
  4. 1, 2, 3, 4.
  5. Timing Is Everything.
  6. What Could Possibly Have Gone Wrong?
  7. AECI.
  8. The Public Information Alone Could Suggest Slower Speedup.
  9. Well, That Escalated Quickly.
  10. This Infinite Series Likely Has a Finite Sum.
  11. We Cannot Say What We Cannot Say.
  12. Study of Anthropic’s Compute Allocation Was Postponed.
  13. Security Mindset.
  14. It’s a Secret to Everyone.
  15. Review of the Risk Report from August 2026.
  16. A Word From Our Cofounder.
  17. People Update Their Timelines and Expectations.
  18. You Are Not Ready.
  19. If (If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies) Then Don’t Let Anyone Build It.
  20. How Can We Legally Define RSI?

Top Conclusions

This is how they describe their subjective conclusions.

METR: In our first section, we share our subjective conclusions about risk. We now believe that:

  • As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate.
  • A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025.
  • The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks.

Here are their top empirical findings:

  • Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.
  • We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute.
  • Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.
  • We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment.

Data Access and Redactions

The goal of the report was to measure acceleration of Anthropic’s internal growth rate, how much of that acceleration is due to AI R&D and whether there exist any important bottlenecks to further acceleration. This requires a lot of sensitive data, and they got most of what they requested.

They could access:

A detailed description of the data we had access to was redacted. A summarized version is as follows:

  1. Internal benchmark scores and AECI for internal models, plus sample tasks, rubric answers and agent expenditure on those tasks.
  2. Historical data on algorithmic efficiency and overall model strength in pretraining and RL, as well as improvements to compute utilization, inference efficiency and data efficiency.
  3. Headcount and attribution of progress to specific staff.
  4. Training compute metrics in many relevant domains.
  5. Internal analysis on relevant open questions.
  6. Internal surveys of self-reported AI uplift by team.
  7. Lines of code and pull requests across the company and some research teams.
  8. AI agent inference spend over time.
  9. Internal documents on autonomous research contributions.
  10. ~15 interviews with key staff, covering a predefined but wide scope that excluded particularly sensitive topics.

In a small number of cases, Anthropic did not provide relevant information when they deemed it too sensitive.​

Anthropic also offered extensive staff time and expertise to this project. We believe the two staff we worked most closely with are the two highest-context researchers on AI R&D acceleration measurement at Anthropic. Both of these staff met with us frequently for live discussion, and spent substantial time collecting data, doing analysis, and providing feedback.

In exchange, Anthropic could redact anything in the report. They did so, aggressively.

METR’s only recourse is that it can then share its level of access, that things had been redacted, and whether findings depend on redacted information. Which they do. The majority of the most informative evidence is redacted.

METR: We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative. As a consequence, the public must rely on our judgment more than we consider ideal.

Some of these redactions seem clearly appropriate. Others seem questionable.

METR: While we were able to freely share our highest-level conclusions about risk, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.”

Some of these redactions are themselves challenging to describe clearly without revealing sensitive information we have been asked to redact.

We share a table of important evidence we were and were not able to discuss given the redactions in our process section below. All redactions that were important for our conclusions are covered by our descriptions in that table or other in-line descriptions in the report below.

Much of the redacted evidence we viewed had multiple plausible interpretations, and both METR and Anthropic researchers have significant uncertainty about how to synthesize the evidence into a holistic picture. This makes it hard for the public to judge this evidence themselves, reconcile it with evidence from other sources, and come to their own conclusions (i.e. this report does not achieve ‘transparency about evidence’). As a consequence, the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here.

METR: Anthropic’s redactions also meant that we could not communicate:

  1. Our more detailed estimates of acceleration and attribution to AI usage for key areas of the model training pipeline.
  2. Our more detailed breakdown of progress attributable to compute, data and algorithmic progress, other than the key takeaway that “We are confident that the acceleration was not due to acceleration in training compute.”
  3. More detailed answers to the limitations questions in our proposal, which would require more discussion of methodological details.
  4. Forecasts of metrics for future models.

They also made some other more minor redactions throughout, which we attempt to describe in each section of this report.

Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.”

They also could not show us any use of METR’s core accounting framework. We know the framework looks like this, but that’s all we get:

The Pace of Progress

This is one of the more annoying redactions. What are these non-AI factors? Candidates include compute scaling, hiring, data improvements, algorithmic discoveries and resolving other bottlenecks. Compute has been ruled out. But we don’t know how they view the other factors.

METR:

  1. The acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors. We investigated a variety of factors which could have contributed to the observed acceleration in late 2025, but details of many of these factors have been redacted.
  2. We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI. This judgment is given with substantial uncertainty, but is based on a variety of lines of evidence on contributions from AI and other causes. We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time, and do not think the other factors we investigated would explain the sustained acceleration. The evidence of speedup from the usage of AI we describe below also seems compatible with a large contribution.​

The non-AI acceleration continues, supplemented by the AI-driven one:

Thus they illustrate how to think about all three numbers: The historic trend, the counterfactual no-AI trend and the observed trend that includes use of AI.

1, 2, 3, 4

The Risk Report introduced Model 1 and Model 2. Now we meet 3 and 4, and also 5.

This includes the following models (these are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames):

  • Unreleased 2022, which finished training in 2022
  • Model 2, which finished training in July 2026
  • Model 3, which finished training in August–September 2026
  • Model 4, which finished training in September–October 2026

METR’s Full Report includes a forecast for a future model, but this was redacted.

Timing Is Everything

If this is consistent, it seems like the clear correct way:

METR: We use the date at which the model could be used by most Anthropic employees instead of public release dates; this allows us to make apples-to-apples comparisons with unreleased models. These in general show slightly higher degrees of acceleration as Anthropic is holding onto more recent models for slightly longer before their public release.

OpenAI used to hold onto models for a longer time. Then it got shorter. Whereas after Mythos, various forces are now holding models back for longer, including the desire to keep an advantage in R&D.

There are different reasons one might want to measure ‘leads’ or rates of progress. If you are measuring for commercial purposes, you care mostly about practical questions of what a public customer can do when. If you are measuring to predict RSI, you care about a very different measurement, and what you care about are internal capabilities, and ability to use them to make progress at the frontier.

By that measure, things are picking up faster, and also the gaps are wider. If you believe in what this report is telling us, these are the measurements that count.

What Could Possibly Have Gone Wrong?

There are a number of ways this could be wrong, or be less than ideally accurate.

The biggest issue is limited access to data. Not all data requests were accepted and there are many documents and other information sources that were not available.

METR might have missed further acceleration, or AECI could underestimate capability growth, or automation could be closer.

On the other hand, perhaps there are non-AI factors that were missed that explain past acceleration, or historical growth was unusually low creating the illusion of fundamental acceleration. Or perhaps acceleration could only work on a narrow set of tasks.

I notice that the upside risks and downside risks of the estimate are asymmetrical. We have three in each direction but they don’t match (Opus 5.5 says some of these do cancel out, but I don’t think they fully do, and others clearly don’t):

  1. Acceleration might be missed but not illusory.
  2. AECI could underestimate effective growth but not overestimate it, although elsewhere they do discuss error in both directions.
  3. Automation could be closer but not farther away.
  4. Historical growth might be unusually low, but not unusually high.
  5. Acceleration could be narrower, but not broader.
  6. Non-AI factors could be underestimated but not overestimated.

Curves on such things do not have to be symmetrical, so long as the average results of all of them are incorporated. This doesn’t have to be an error. I do still wonder.

AECI

The main metric METR uses for this report is the Anthropic fork of the Epoch Capabilities Index, AECI.

AECI is a measure of practical capability. Growth in AECI is multiplicative of odds of success on a task rather than linear, so linear progress on AECI means more than you might think:

Charles Foster (METR): It’s easy to mistake linear gains in ECI for linear gains in model performance. Each additional point actually *multiplies* a model’s odds of success on every benchmark. For example, historically each 5-point increase in ECI corresponded to roughly a doubling in time horizon.

METR focused a lot on the question of whether the metrics are biased or consistent.

METR: These investigations included attempts to understand:

  1. Different methodological variants of internal metrics. We spent multiple weeks on these investigations, and this is our greatest source of uncertainty.
  2. The beliefs of staff on the relevant teams about key internal evidence and estimates of acceleration.
  3. Whether other parts of the model training pipeline could be biasing our estimates of acceleration, and where adjustments could be applied.
  4. Whether Anthropic could be overfitting to internal metrics.

The measurements are also robust to choice of included benchmarks, and to which model snapshots are included, and to regularization.

If non-Anthropic models are included, then the estimate of acceleration goes down to 1.4x.

METR suggests as another potential justification for lower acceleration rates that Anthropic’s models underperformed on benchmarks in the earlier period relative to their true capabilities, which matches my understanding.

I would also suggest that if Anthropic was previously behind, then being behind makes progress easier via fast following, even if you cannot distill.

There are some potential issues with AECI:

  1. We go into detail on potential problems with AECI such as:
    1. Anthropic’s internal benchmarks are increasingly saturated: Model 4 achieves greater than 50% on all the AECI benchmarks on which it was tested. However, measured acceleration appears reasonably robust to saturation concerns.
    2. Token spend may be too low to maximally elicit models.
    3. The logistic link function could be misspecified on a few benchmarks. However, on the whole we think it is a reasonable approximation.
    4. There are various reasons why an acceleration in benchmark scores could overstate or understate an acceleration in real-world impacts.

If AECI is going to serve as a measure of the capabilities of models, the first part of this must be true:

AECI assumes that a model’s score on a benchmark is a function of the model’s latent strength, and specifically that the function is logistic (shown below in black).

Any given metric then has to worry about S-curves and saturation points.

This can be interpreted as an assumption on the distribution of difficulty of tasks in a benchmark, including how many tasks are broken or what fraction can be guessed. The following figure illustrates a few different link functions. The logistic function assumes a symmetric distribution with exponentially declining tails. The log-log function assumes a long tail of hard tasks; the complementary log-log function assumes a long tail of easy tasks.

Depending on what type of curve you think this is, you get different measurements of the rate of acceleration. Unfortunately basically all the curve fits are similarly good at Out-of-sample R2. It makes sense to default to standard logistic, but this illustrates that in theory you can explain or justify a wide range of measurements.

METR says they have no reason to prefer one of these over others. I would say they make distinct claims over the distribution of tasks. So if we want to know which is best, we should look at the tasks.

The Public Information Alone Could Suggest Slower Speedup

In particular, if you are relying only on the AECI, one can selectively edit out the Mythos jump or consider part of this catching up on relative compute allocation.

Toby Ord: I don’t think 2x is the best interpretation of this data. It assumes zero level shift from the new Mythos pre-train. If you allow for a level shift from that as well as a slope change, the slope change drops to about 1.4x.

METR has released a very interesting report suggesting a recent acceleration in AI capabilities this year at Anthropic due to RSI.
But they can’t confidently reject an alternative explanation: the step change you get with the larger pre-train of Mythos.

Woody Lee: It looks like Anthropic was running behind the composite frontier so the speed up in relation to that is 1.4x not sure if this changed any analysis, but it shows that using just the ant baseline may give a different number.

There are two responses to this. One is that there is private redacted information that is factoring into the reports.

Buck Shlegeris: Toby’s analysis totally misses the point here IMO. He’s right that the graph of capabilities over time could be explained as a one-off jump in capabilities from the Mythos pretrain. But that graph is not the main reason why METR thinks AI R&D is now sped up 1.7x by AI. The graph is just the only part of their analysis that wasn’t redacted.

They say that “a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI”, based on “a variety of lines of evidence on contributions from AI and other causes”, after saying that “[t]he acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors.”

METR’s report makes it clear that they considered Toby’s hypothesis and rejected it for redacted reasons, rather than failing to consider it, in the appendix “New internal models make a permanent slope change look more plausible than a one-time jump at Mythos Preview.”

It totally makes sense to worry that METR’s analysis is wrong. It’s definitely unfortunate that the main evidence they were allowed to share does not suffice to demonstrate their point, for this reason among others. But I don’t think it makes sense to consider Toby’s argument a knockdown argument against the report’s conclusion, because the conclusion wasn’t mostly derived from the observations whose interpretation Toby disputes. See [here].

The other response is that such modifications are selective. Yes, if you take away whatever the biggest discontinuous improvement is over a period, you will see slower returns. Yes, Anthropic’s position in compute consumption relative to others has shifted. But once we go down such roads, why do we think similar shifts will not happen again?

There is always temptation to extrapolate a future without such jumps. You don’t get to do that. The baseline scenario contains outliers and jumps.

We can only reject the Mythos upshift if we have strong reason to believe we won’t be able to do any similar things again. I don’t see why that would be true.

Well, That Escalated Quickly

It is poised to soon escalate far more quickly. This fact is overdetermined. There are even ‘signs of life’ of areas of potentially full automation. The details are less clear.

METR: We define AI speedup as the ratio between a staff member or team’s output with AI and without AI, noting that output can often be difficult to measure or define.

We now briefly survey the overall evidence for AI speedup, concluding:

  1. There is some evidence for high speedup, though the precise amount of speedup is highly uncertain.
  2. Fully autonomous contributions to AI R&D are not currently a large contributor to overall progress, but they may be in the near future.

… We have many lines of evidence relevant to AI’s contribution to progress in different parts of the model training pipeline, including interviews, self-reported uplift, headcount, lines of code, experiment usage, and qualitative reflections from leadership. We highlight three important unredacted sources.

  1. Both METR and Anthropic interviewed many researchers in detail about the degree of overall acceleration in their area of work attributable to AI use (see details in the appendix below). Our overall impression was a quite wide range of estimates, but centered around a 2x acceleration.
  2. Anthropic also shared data on self-reported uplift due to AI from a variety of sources. The most recent data is from a series of Slack polls. … The responses reflect low-effort consideration. Nevertheless, we observe consistent growth in these self-reports, and very high levels (reaching 12x in October 2026), as shown in the chart below.
  3. Researchers described significant “signs of life” implying [highly significant and fully autonomous] contributions could occur soon.

The estimates here are a lot more than 2x in uplift for the employees, offset by slowness elsewhere, balancing out to 2x. Coding is dramatically more productive now.

Ajeya Cotra (METR): Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that.

Ajeya Cotra (METR): researcher labor is only one input to discovering these compute multipliers

… If we assume a very simple Cobb-Douglas model where experiment compute and labor are similarly important, that means the uplift to labor roughly needs to be the square of the acceleration in compute multipliers.

… This would imply that we would need a (~2-3x)^2 = ~4-9x speed up in labor to make overall AI capabilities go twice as fast.

They call this ‘broadly support AI doubling the growth rate’ but if we are going purely by the Claude sentiment analysis then the median answer was ‘borderline/unclear’:

Both METR and Anthropic interviewed many researchers (see details in the following section). We used Claude to classify the quotes according to whether they support 2x or more acceleration from AI in their area of work, relative to working without AI. We interpret the results as mildly in favor of 2x or greater acceleration:

  • Yes: 2
  • Leans yes: 3
  • Borderline/unclear: 4
  • Leans no: 0
  • No: 2

The quotes, with sensitive details redacted, are in the following section.

Congressman Greg Casar: Ban RSI.

Andrew Curran: It’s going to be an interesting couple of years.

Arthur B.: Only if they ban RSI

Even Neil Chilson sees little innovation harm in ‘banning RSI’ because, by his definition, no one would be so stupid as to do it and not keep humans ‘in the loop.’

Neil Chilson: I see little innovation harm from an RSI ban, for my definition of RSI. Little innovation harm because RSI, properly defined, is a practice too stupid to need banning. But I’m worried Alex means something different than me.

Daniel Filan: What’s your definition of RSI?

Neil Chilson: Something like “fully relinquishing AI R&D and deployment to AI, with no ability to monitor and stop the process.”

Which by the Sixth Law of Human Stupidity means we will definitely do it at the first opportunity if allowed to do so, also the AI companies are screaming that they are going to do it at the first opportunity if allowed to do so.

Neil and I agree it would be deeply stupid, but for very different reasons.

How Can We Legally Define RSI?

You cannot ban that which you cannot define.

Banning an overly narrow definition, such as Neil’s above, won’t make us not dead.

If you so narrowly define and ban RSI as meaning only a 100% relinquishing with zero ability to monitor, what you get is a 90% then 99% then 99.9% automated process with some illusion that you can monitor and stop the process. Then you find out you cannot stop the process and that your human is not in any of the loops that matter. Then, probably, you die.

Legal text has to be robust to various workarounds, including in very stupid ways, as in Critch might well have a point here no matter how stupid it sounds when you say it:

Andrew Critch: This ban [on RSI] needs to be expanded to “Recursively Self-Modifying”, to avoid unfortunate debates about whether killing or driving humans to extinction counts as “Improvement”. (Answer: it doesn’t, but many people disturbingly claim it does.)

The problem with most other known definitions is they don’t work as legal text.

Alex Bores: Every AI company is trying to fully automate AI research; to allow the AIs to build the next AI.

This is called Recursive Self Improvement (RSI).

… The exact mechanism can be debated. The ban doesn’t have to be permanent either (see below for both). This is not the only thing we have to do in regards to AI, far from it! But it is urgent. Congress must ban RSI.

Woody Lee (responding to Chilson from above): [Alex Bores] defines what he means [by RSI] in the tweet.

Neil Chilson: That’s not a definition that works in legislation.

Dave Kasten: I often disagree with Neil, so I want to flag here that I STRONGLY agree with him: we desperately need a definition of RSI that has gone through a bunch of rounds of lawyers kicking its tires.

You’re a law student, want to get cited for forever? Write this as your journal note.

Saul Munn: wdyt of @testingham et al’s definition of ‘self-sustaining acceleration’?

Dave Kasten: Seems interesting, but not leg text by a long shot

It is probably going to be impossible to come up with a definition that will stop RSI at an early enough stage that such a law stays relevant to what happens next, and also avoids hitting anything that is not RSI. The blast radius will not be zero.

The good news is that the blast radius can be things that RSI skeptics mostly say will not happen either way. If they are in good faith, they should be happy to draw lines in the sand that they do not expect anyone to be able to cross.

This is similar to the talk of ‘pacing the frontier.’ Those calling to Pace the Frontier want to go at High Speed rather than Ludicrous Speed. Those who are against it want to ensure we go at Medium Speed rather than Low Speed, would love High Speed, and are scared of pausing entirely. It is easy to see how a deal there could be win-win.

Now more than ever, we need to prepare for scenarios where the critical events happen in 2027 or 2028. It might not play out that way, but it very well might.
